title: Tenali Raman Tale 72

full_text:
King Krishnadevaraya, pleased by the gentle touch and pleasant conversation of his personal royal barber, an illiterate man named Keshava, made a whimsical announcement in the royal diwan:
'Keshava has served my head with such delicate skill that I have decided to honor him with the highest title of the realm!
I decree that Keshava shall be appointed Chief Royal Scholar of the Academy, with a salary of three hundred gold coins, and all the court pandits must bow before his wisdom!'

The court scholars were deeply humiliated, but terrified of contradicting the Emperor’s absolute command.
They appealed secretly to Tenali Raman.

Tenali smiled: 'Fear not, revered scholars. Tomorrow, we shall see how easily royal decrees can transform nature.'

The next morning, while King Krishnadevaraya was riding toward the river for his morning worship, he saw an extraordinary sight on the riverbank:
Tenali Raman was standing in the water with a scrawny, black street dog.
Tenali was vigorously scrubbing the dog with a rough stone, rubbing fragrant sandalwood paste into its fur, and chanting Sanskrit mantras at the top of his voice!

The King stopped his horse in astonishment:
'Tenali! What on earth are you doing to that dirty street dog in the sacred river?'

Tenali bowed with solemn respect:
'Jahanpanah! I am performing the Sacred Rite of Equine Transformation!
I am washing this street dog with holy water and sandalwood to turn it into a magnificent, pedigree Arabian warhorse for Your Majesty’s cavalry!'

The King stared at Tenali as though he had lost his mind:
'Tenali, art thou mad? No amount of scrubbing, sandalwood, or chanting can ever turn a dog into a horse! Nature cannot be changed by wishful washing!'

Tenali looked up at the King with piercing, sparkling wit:
'Indeed, Your Majesty! If no amount of scrubbing can turn a dog into a horse, how can a single royal decree turn an illiterate barber into a Chief Scholar of the Academy?
Scholarship requires decades of disciplined study, contemplation, and learning. When a king awards academic titles based on flattery rather than merit, he makes a mockery of learning and disgraces his empire!'

King Krishnadevaraya felt the sharp sting of truth in Tenali’s brilliant analogy.
He burst into appreciative laughter, revoked the barber’s academic appointment, and instead rewarded Keshava with a generous gift of gold and a comfortable house for his barber services.
The scholars cheered Tenali, who preserved the integrity of learning through the power of satire.
moral: True scholarship is earned through diligent study, not through royal decrees or superficial titles.
